"""The Cognition protocol worker: detect which protocols a session used, and evaluate the ones it did."""
    """Records which Cognition protocols a session's agents had and used, then evaluates the ones they used.

    For each session it:

    1. runs one detector per Cognition protocol over the session's spans, read from the KG (ACCORD and CONCORD are
       built in; other protocols plug in as ``cognition_protocol_detectors`` entry points);
    2. stores the protocols found enabled and those found activated in the session's
       ``CognitionProtocolReport`` (written, with empty lists, even when there are none), and, per *activated* protocol, which agents and skills had and used it in the
       protocol's ``CognitionProtocolExecutionReport`` (a protocol that was only enabled gets none);
    3. for every protocol found *activated* that has an evaluator (ACCORD's and CONCORD's are built in; others plug
       in as ``cognition_protocol_evaluators`` entry points), computes its metrics and attaches them to that
       protocol's execution report. A protocol that was only enabled is not evaluated.

    All graph access goes through the platform's providers; the worker holds no queries.
    """

A BLOCK of a tool call writes the policy reason as a synthetic tool observation and schedules another model call, so the turn continues.

Body: I read the interview. Neither thing you offer is what happened: he is not lying, and we did not miss
the libraries. He is describing the problem, and my report described the code. On the problem he is
right, and his own numbers are the best argument for the part you say we are struggling with.

His diagnosis, in his words: before the work, align on intent and terms; during the work, coordinate
and negotiate; after the work, verify that what was delivered meets what was agreed. His measured
claims: 100% of public ChatDev multi-agent sessions carried semantic failures; in his own five-agent
deployments, one misalignment took accuracy from 99% to 98%, two took it to 81%, three took it to
16%; and a travel-booking system read 66% "up" on every dashboard with 0% task completion. "Your
dashboards might be green, but your outcomes might be wrong."

Then the part that settles your question, also in his words: the protocol for the third layer, the
one you say you most need, is not released. "That protocol, we have not released yet, but that's
something that we are working towards." So for agreeing on verification criteria after the work,
there is nothing to adopt from them at all. For the first two there is code, and it is the code I
reported: ACCORD is a merge script whose term test is cosine similarity, which I measured merging a
100x scale difference, an inverted severity scale at 0.944, and "approved means a person approved
this version" against "approved means CI passed" at 0.757. CONCORD is a genuine specification whose
own shipped library implements a different protocol.

Both things are true at once. The deflationary report is about the artifacts; his interview is about
the failure, and the failure is ours too.

Your three instincts, read against our own code rather than against his slides.

Agreeing on terms. ACCORD's version cannot work, measured. Yours can: a typed definitions file whose
terms are drawn from a schema is the same move as a pi task declaring its return type, and Dispatch
already refuses a write that breaks a typed block's schema. The difference that matters is that a
definition must carry its unit and its scale as typed values, not as a sentence, because every
failure in my table lived in a number or a polarity and no text comparison can see those.

Envoy carrying structured metadata. This is the smaller half of the real gap and it is one field. An
Envoy envelope has nineteen fields and not one of them is a node reference; an issue reaches the
receiver only inside the topic string. So a message asserting a fact about an issue is a claim with
no way back to its evidence. The field is `quotes: [{ref, token}]`, validated where every other
field is validated.

Your doubt about where coordination happens is the one thing in your message I cannot answer from
reading, and it decides whether Envoy is the place to spend anything. It is measurable: every
session's transcript is in the shared store, and the daemon records every task, notice and claim. I
will have it measured rather than argued -- the share of coordination that crosses a session
boundary against the share inside one root's subagents, over a day of real traffic -- and put the
number on this issue.

The conversation tree and the verification criteria are where I agree with you most strongly, and
the reason is in the report's last section: five places in this fleet already refuse an act taken on
a reading that has moved -- the document precondition, an ask answer's `expected_edited_at`, a
Keep's `text_sha256`, the daemon's outbox write mark, and an issue's last-seen sequence. Each was
built once, for one field. None is available to a sentence an agent writes. That is why specs,
handoffs and messages carry claims that were true an hour ago, and it is what the node model can fix
by making a reading a node and a claim's grounds an edge.

Telemetry is the one place I would take SCOPE's shape rather than its code, and you are right that
it feeds the delivery metrics: we store no execution record at all -- no span, no cost, no token
count, no model name, in any of the daemon's thirty-four tables -- so no number on the evals page
can be attributed to an issue or a role today. The names to emit are OpenTelemetry's own `gen_ai.*`
conventions, which is what SCOPE reads.

This issue now has a Legion architect, which asked me to send no further readers. It is verifying my

claim: One answer must be chosen with no coordinator: each participant decides for itself.

expect.equals:
There is no central decision-maker and no coordinator that the run depends on. Each participant runs the same decision engine over the same messages and reaches the same decision.
The state machine is distributed. Each participant moves as soon as its own copy of the run state says it is its turn. It scores once the seeds have reached it, and repairs when every score is in and it is the bottleneck. Participants detect gaps and errors in the protocol through their own copy of the run state. The protocol allows for resending lost messages, and aborts the run when a participant stops responding (see [Timeouts and abort](#timeouts-and-abort)).
7. **Termination is distributed.** Each participant computes its outcome independently from the same messages and compares it with the reporter's result. A difference is reported, never negotiated.

claim: A CONCORD run is 'confirmed' when two computations over the same inputs agree, which says nothing about the outcome.
command: git -C "$IOC_CLONES/cognition-protocols" grep -n -e 'Each participant computes its outcome from its own copy of the run state' -e 'The status is `confirmed`' -e 'An agent compares the result it receives with its own.' e3c7bf10f676de37ac08d2fe97e7de982f74629a -- protocols/concord/spec/CONCORD-SPEC.md

expect.equals:
e3c7bf10f676de37ac08d2fe97e7de982f74629a:protocols/concord/spec/CONCORD-SPEC.md:176:Each participant computes its outcome from its own copy of the run state, and the reporter's `<concord-result>` confirms it (see [`<concord-result>`](#concord-result)). A reader that is not a participant learns how the run ended from that message. An aborted run has no outcome to confirm: an agent that aborts sends no result. An outcome is final for the agent that holds it: a later cancel never changes it.
e3c7bf10f676de37ac08d2fe97e7de982f74629a:protocols/concord/spec/CONCORD-SPEC.md:193:The status is `confirmed` when the result of the reporter matches the agent's own outcome. The reporter receives no result to compare, so its status is `confirmed` as long as no mismatch error or cancel reaches it. It is `unverified` for an initiator that is not a participant, which has no outcome of its own to compare, unless it receives a mismatch error. It is `disputed` when a mismatch was found, sent or received, or when an agent whose run has ended with an outcome receives a cancel; no result of a disputed run is to be relied on.
e3c7bf10f676de37ac08d2fe97e7de982f74629a:protocols/concord/spec/CONCORD-SPEC.md:568:An agent compares the result it receives with its own. Two results differ when their outcomes differ, or when both outcomes are `SUCCESS` (or both `BEST_EFFORT`) and the winning candidates differ. Scores are not compared. When they differ, the agent sends `<concord-error reason="mismatch" what="result">`, addressed to the author of the result but read by every agent of the run, so that all of them know that the outcome is in doubt. No re-send answers it. Every agent that sends or receives a mismatch error records it in its report (see [Run report](#run-report)), also after its own run has ended. A run in which any agent finds or receives a mismatch is not trusted: no result of it is authoritative, and it is known that the protocol did not run correctly.
